\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:responding}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how someone is in Telugu, answer naturally, and return the question.}

After the name comes the exchange everyone actually has — and, for the first time, a Telugu verb “to be.” \te{మీరు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నారు}? / \te{నేను} \te{బాగున్నాను}, \te{ధన్యవాదములు}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[3]{\te{౩} — the Telugu numeral for 3}

\label{lesson:TE-S142-digit-3}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ం} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{◌్}?

One numeral this time, and it is read the way every numeral is read: as an amount.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{౩}}
\textbf{\te{౩}} is \textbf{three}.

Three of the ten. Read the row below left to right and say the values out loud in your own language — \textbf{one, two, three}. Saying the value rather than a Telugu word is not a shortcut around the language; it is what a numeral is for.

Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\section[elā]{\te{ఎలా} (elā) — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} another of the e- questions}

\label{lesson:TE-C03-elaa}



\begin{quote}
You met \textbf{\te{ఏమిటి}} (\emph{ēmiṭi}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) in Chapter 2. Here is its sibling — and, like all of Telugu's question-words, it begins with \textbf{e-}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Telugu.)} \textbf{\te{ఎ}} (independent short \emph{e}) + \textbf{\te{లా}} (\emph{lā}, \emph{la} + the long-\emph{ā} sign) $\to$ \textbf{\te{ఎలా}} (\emph{elā}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{ఎలా}} (\emph{elā}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, on the interrogative base \textbf{\te{ఎ}-} (\emph{e-}) you already met in \emph{ēmiṭi}. Telugu gathers nearly all its questions under this \textbf{e-}: \emph{ēmiṭi} (what), \emph{elā} (how), \emph{evaru} (who), \emph{ekkaḍa} (where), \emph{eppuḍu} (when), \emph{enduku} (why). It is the same Dravidian question-root that heads Tamil's \emph{eppaḍi} and Kannada's \emph{ēnu} — a family older than the Sanskrit words that Telugu otherwise borrows so freely.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{ఎ} (independent short \emph{e}) + \te{లా} (\emph{lā}) $\to$ \te{ఎలా} (\emph{elā}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}elā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the e- question family — \emph{ēmiṭi, elā, evaru, ekkaḍa, eppuḍu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What base do Telugu's question-words share, and which cousins head their own? (The interrogative \emph{e-}; Tamil's \emph{eppaḍi}, Kannada's \emph{ēnu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mīru elā unnāru?]{\te{మీరు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నారు}? (mīru elā unnāru?)}

\label{lesson:TE-C03-miiru-elaa-unnaaru}



\begin{quote}
The everyday \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and the verb \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} that carries it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
The new word is \textbf{\te{ఉన్నారు}} (\emph{unnāru}, \textquotedblleft{}you are/exist\textquotedblright{}): from the verb \textbf{\te{ఉండు}} (\emph{uṇḍu}, \textquotedblleft{}to be, to exist, to stay\textquotedblright{}) + the respectful-you ending \textbf{-\te{ారు}} (\emph{-āru}). Note the doubled \textbf{\te{న్న}} (\emph{nn}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{మీరు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నారు}?} = \textbf{\te{మీరు}} (\emph{mīru}, \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} respectful) + \textbf{\te{ఎలా}} (\emph{elā}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\te{ఉన్నారు}} (\emph{unnāru}, \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}you how are?\textquotedblright{}, the verb \textbf{last}, as in every Telugu sentence. The verb is \textbf{\te{ఉండు}} (\emph{uṇḍu}), \textquotedblleft{}to be / to exist / to stay\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian, and the workhorse behind \textquotedblleft{}how are you,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I'm well,\textquotedblright{} and (you'll see in Chapter 5) \textquotedblleft{}I live.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb carries \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}]
The ending \textbf{-\te{ారు}} (\emph{-āru}) already means \textquotedblleft{}you (respectful),\textquotedblright{} so \emph{mīru} can be dropped: \emph{elā unnāru?} is a complete \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} To a friend (\emph{nuvvu}), the ending changes: \textbf{\te{నువ్వు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నావు}?} (\emph{nuvvu elā unnāvu?} — \emph{-āvu} for the familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}). Match the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to the verb-ending, as Telugu always does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful question — \emph{mīru elā unnāru?}
  \item the familiar version — \emph{nuvvu elā unnāvu?}
  \item the verb and its meaning (\emph{uṇḍu} — \textquotedblleft{}to be / exist / stay\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb powers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}, and how does the ending change for a friend? (\emph{Uṇḍu}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}; \emph{-āru} $\to$ \emph{-āvu} for the familiar \emph{nuvvu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\te{ఉ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\section[nēnu]{\te{నేను} (nēnu) — \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the Dravidian first person}

\label{lesson:TE-C03-nenu}



\begin{quote}
To answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} you first need \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} In Chapter 2 you learned \emph{nā} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}); here is its owner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{నే}} (\emph{nē}, \emph{na} + long-\emph{ē} sign) + \textbf{\te{ను}} (\emph{nu}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{నేను}} (\emph{nēnu}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{నేను}} (\emph{nēnu}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*yāṉ / *nēn} — native, and (unlike Hindi's \emph{maiṁ}, cousin of English \emph{me}) \textbf{not} related to the European \textquotedblleft{}I/me\textquotedblright{} family. Its possessive is the \textbf{\te{నా}} (\emph{nā}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) you already met: \emph{nēnu} \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} \emph{nā} \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{} For all that Telugu borrows Sanskrit vocabulary elsewhere, its most basic pronouns stayed Dravidian to the core — the grammar's foundations never changed hands.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} you can drop}]
Telugu verbs carry the person in their ending — \emph{unnānu} already means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I} am\textquotedblright{} — so \emph{nēnu} is often left out. You still learn it first, because the answer to \emph{elā unnāru?} begins with it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\te{నే} (\emph{nē}) + \te{ను} (\emph{nu}) $\to$ \te{నేను} (\emph{nēnu}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nēnu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \emph{nēnu} (I), \emph{nā} (my)
  \item is it related to English \emph{me}? (No — native Dravidian)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{nēnu}'s possessive, and is Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} cousin to English \emph{me}? (\emph{Nā}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}; no — it is native Dravidian, unlike the borrowed Sanskrit nouns around it.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[bāgā]{\te{బాగా} (bāgā) — \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} and how to answer}

\label{lesson:TE-C03-baagaa}



\begin{quote}
The word that answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and one Telugu says all the time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\te{బా}} (\emph{bā}, \emph{ba} + long \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\te{గా}} (\emph{gā}, \emph{ga} + long \emph{ā}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{బాగా}} (\emph{bāgā}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{బాగా}} (\emph{bāgā}, \textquotedblleft{}well, nicely, very\textquotedblright{}) comes from \textbf{\te{బాగు}} (\emph{bāgu}, \textquotedblleft{}goodness, well-being\textquotedblright{}). It is the everyday \textquotedblleft{}well/good/very much\textquotedblright{}: \emph{bāgā undi} (\textquotedblleft{}it's good\textquotedblright{}), \emph{bāgā ceppāru} (\textquotedblleft{}well said\textquotedblright{}). To answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you,\textquotedblright{} fuse it with the \emph{uṇḍu} verb:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నేను} \te{బాగున్నాను}} (\emph{nēnu bāgunnānu}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am well}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{bāgā} + \emph{unnānu}, \textquotedblleft{}I am,\textquotedblright{} run together).
\end{quote}

The whole exchange:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{mīru elā unnāru?} (\textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{nēnu bāgunnānu, dhanyavādamulu.} (\textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\te{బా} (\emph{bā}) + \te{గా} (\emph{gā}) $\to$ \te{బాగా} (\emph{bāgā}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bāgā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the full reply — \emph{nēnu bāgunnānu}
  \item add thanks (from Chapter 1) — \emph{dhanyavādamulu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the full reply to \emph{mīru elā unnāru?}. (\emph{Nēnu bāgunnānu} — \emph{bāgā} \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} fused with \emph{unnānu} \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ra]{\te{ర} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S06-letter-ra}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{౪} — what amount does it stand for? And one from further back: \te{◌ం}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ర}}
\textbf{\te{ర}} — \emph{ra}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{r}, it is \textbf{ra}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{ర} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{సరే}} \emph{sarē} — okay / alright (sarē)
  \item \textbf{\te{పేరు}} \emph{pēru} — name
  \item \textbf{\te{నువ్వు} / \te{మీరు}} \emph{nuvvu / mīru} — you (familiar / respectful)
\end{itemize}

\section[paravālēdu]{\te{పరవాలేదు} (paravālēdu) — \textquotedblleft{}no problem\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C03-paravaaledu}



\begin{quote}
When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply, and it is built on a word you met in Chapter 1.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Two joined words: \textbf{\te{పరవా}} (\emph{paravā}, \textquotedblleft{}harm, concern\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\te{లేదు}} (\emph{lēdu}, \textquotedblleft{}there is not\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} (\emph{paravālēdu}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{there is no harm}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{paravā} (\textquotedblleft{}harm, concern\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\te{లేదు}} (\emph{lēdu}, \textquotedblleft{}is-not / there-is-not\textquotedblright{}), the Chapter-1 negative. It serves as \textquotedblleft{}it's okay / no worries / never mind / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} The key atom, \textbf{\te{లేదు}} (\emph{lēdu}), is where Telugu goes its own way: Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam all say \emph{illa(i)} for \textquotedblleft{}is-not,\textquotedblright{} but \textbf{Telugu alone} uses \textbf{\te{లేదు}} (\emph{lēdu}) — so Tamil's \textquotedblleft{}no problem\textquotedblright{} is \emph{paravāyillai}, and Telugu's is \emph{paravālēdu}, the same idea built on each language's own \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{} One phrase shows both the Dravidian bond and the one place Telugu breaks from its sisters.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \te{లేదు}, Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{}}]
\emph{Lēdu} negates existence: \emph{ḍabbu lēdu} (\textquotedblleft{}there's no money\textquotedblright{}), \emph{ēmī lēdu} (\textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{}). It is the negative twin of \textbf{\te{ఉంది}} (\emph{undi}, \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}) and of the \emph{uṇḍu} verb behind \textquotedblleft{}how are you.\textquotedblright{} Learn \emph{undi} / \emph{lēdu} together — \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}there is not.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}paravālēdu\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}there is no harm\textquotedblright{})
  \item the Telugu \textquotedblleft{}is-not\textquotedblright{} that sets it apart from Tamil (\emph{lēdu}, vs. Tamil \emph{illai})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{paravālēdu} literally say, and how does its \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} differ from Tamil's? (\textquotedblleft{}There is no harm\textquotedblright{}; Telugu uses \emph{lēdu} where Tamil/Kannada/Malayalam use \emph{illa(i)}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[5]{\te{౫} — the Telugu numeral for 5}

\label{lesson:TE-S144-digit-5}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ర} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{౩}?

One numeral this time, and it is read the way every numeral is read: as an amount.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{౫}}
\textbf{\te{౫}} is \textbf{five}.

Half the set. Everything the book has shown you so far is on the row below, in no order at all.

\subsection*{Writing: \te{౫} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{౫} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this row and say the value of each numeral in it, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{౫}  ·  \te{౩}  ·  \te{౧}  ·  \te{౪}  ·  \te{౨}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{౫} three times, saying \textquotedblleft{}5\textquotedblright{} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} for \te{౫} on any page of a Telugu book, calendar or doorplate you can find
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which numeral is this — \te{౫}? What amount does it stand for? (\te{౫} is 5.)

One more, from much earlier: \te{◌ే} — what does it do?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 3 — The how-are-you exchange}

\label{lesson:TE-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole responding cycle, from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Read the whole cycle off the page first — Telugu, then the sound, then the sense:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{మీరు} \te{ఎలా} \te{ఉన్నారు}?} & \emph{mīru elā unnāru} & How are you? \\
\textbf{\te{నేను} \te{బాగున్నాను}, \te{ధన్యవాదములు}.} & \emph{nēnu bāgunnānu, dhanyavādamulu} & I'm well, thank you. \\
\textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}.} & \emph{paravālēdu} & No problem / you're welcome. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A few of these characters have not had their own lesson yet. They are here to be \textbf{recognised}, not decoded — the romanization beside each line is what you read from. The letters catch up in the chapters ahead.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} (respectful) — \emph{mīru elā unnāru?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nēnu bāgunnānu, dhanyavādamulu.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}No problem / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{paravālēdu.}
  \item the familiar version of the question — \emph{nuvvu elā unnāvu?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the atoms}]
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the e- question-word for \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} (\emph{elā})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} and the verb \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nēnu}, \emph{uṇḍu})
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}there is / there is not\textquotedblright{} pair (\emph{undi} / \emph{lēdu})
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Roots you now carry:}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{elā} $\leftarrow$ the interrogative \emph{e-} (native Dravidian, like Tamil \emph{eppaḍi})
  \item \emph{nēnu} $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian (unrelated to English \emph{me}); possessive \emph{nā}
  \item \emph{bāgā} $\leftarrow$ \emph{bāgu} \textquotedblleft{}goodness\textquotedblright{}; \emph{nēnu bāgunnānu} \textquotedblleft{}I'm well\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{lēdu} — Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}is-not,\textquotedblright{} where its sisters use \emph{illa(i)}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A stranger asks \emph{mīru elā unnāru?} — give a full, polite reply, and answer their thanks. (\emph{Nēnu bāgunnānu, dhanyavādamulu} — and to thanks, \emph{paravālēdu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
